paragraphs.en: We stayed again. Rising in the morning I opened the window: the long rain had cleared gloriously. A gentle wind turned from time to time, and the sunlight was bright and clear. One could foretell the midday heat. Pomegranate blossoms lay over the ground, melting into red mud; hydrangeas were wet with dew, and jade-hairpin lilies thrust up like snow. From before the gate came the sound of flutes, reed-pipes, cymbals and gongs; I hurried out to look, and it was a wedding party coming to fetch the bride. There were six pairs of painted gauze lanterns, a pair of blue canopies, a pair of red canopies, a pair of flutes, a pair of reed-pipes, a pair of oboes, a pair of double gongs; in the middle four men carried on their shoulders a blue-roofed sedan chair, glass-paned for windows on all four sides, with coloured silk tassels dangling from the four corners. The carrying-pole ran through the middle of the chair, and a large rope of blue silk was bound crosswise about the pole at front and rear, and then a short pole was passed through the middle of the binding, with both ends carried on the shoulders. Four men, eight hooves, in single file and treading heel to heel, neither jolting nor swaying, the chair seeming to float in the air: a splendid method! Behind the chair were two carts, each roofed in black cloth and drawn by one donkey. One cart carried four old women together, their faces all old and ugly yet not forgoing rouge and powder, the hair on the crown entirely gone, bald and reddish-shining as a gourd, an inch of topknot pointing north and yet stuffed full of flowers, earrings dangling from both ears, black jackets and yellow skirts. The other cart carried three young women, in red or green trousers, none wearing skirts. Among them one young girl had considerable beauty. I take it that the old ones were the bride's dressers and wet-nurses, and the young ones maidservants. Thirty-odd riders crowded around a fat, burly lout with scattered black whiskers by his mouth and chin, temporarily wearing a nine-clawed python robe, on a white horse with a gold saddle, his feet steady in silver stirrups, his face heaped with smiles. Behind came two or three carts loaded full of clothing.

paragraphs.orig: 余問店主, 「此邨裏可有秀才塾師麽。」 店主曰, 「邨僻少去處, 那有學究先生, 去年秋間 偶有一個秀才, 從稅官京裡來的, 一路上染得暑痢。 落留此間, 多賴此處人, 一力調治, 經冬徂春, 快得痊可。那先生文章出世, 兼得會寫滿州字情願。 暫住此間, 開了一兩年黌堂, 敎授些此邨小孩們。 以酬救療大恩, 現今坐在了關聖廟堂裡。」 余曰, 「可得主人暫勞鄕導。」 店主曰, 「不必仰人指導。」 擧手指之曰, 「這個屋頭出首的大廟堂是也。」 余問, 「這個先生姓甚名誰。」 店主曰, 「一邨坊都叫他富先生。」 余問, 「富先生多少年紀。」 店主曰 ,「大公子儞自去問他。」 店主因走入炕裡, 手拿紅紙數十片拈示。 道,「此乃那富先生親手墨蹟。」 那紅紙左沿, 細書,「某位舍親尊台, 某年月日, 恭請台駕, 電莅敝筵。」 店主道, 「俺門兄弟, 前春招婿時, 倩他請席。」 刺紙大約, 僅能成字, 而數十紙所寫字樣, 無大無小, 如珠貫絲, 如印一板。
paragraphs.reading: 여문점주, 「차촌리가유수재숙사마.」 점주왈, 「촌벽소거처, 나유학구선생, 거년추간 우유일개수재, 종세관경리내적, 일로상염득서리. 낙류차간, 다뢰차처인, 일력조치, 경동조춘, 쾌득전가. 나선생문장출세, 겸득회사만주자정원. 잠주차간, 개료일량년횡당, 교수사차촌소해문. 이수구료대은, 현금좌재료관성묘당리.」 여왈, 「가득주인잠노향도.」 점주왈, 「불필앙인지도.」 거수지지왈, 「저개옥두출수적대묘당시야.」 여문, 「저개선생성심명수.」 점주왈, 「일촌방도규타부선생.」 여문, 「부선생다소연기.」 점주왈,「대공자이자거문타.」 점주인주입항리, 수나홍지수십편념시. 도,「차내나부선생친수묵적.」 나홍지좌연, 세서,「모위사친존태, 모년월일, 공청태가, 전이폐연.」 점주도, 「엄문형제, 전춘초서시, 천타청석.」 자지대약, 근능성자, 이수십지소사자양, 무대무소, 여주관사, 여인일판.
paragraphs.en: I asked the innkeeper, "Is there a scholar or a village schoolteacher in this hamlet?" The innkeeper said, "The village is out of the way and there are few places to go; where would we have a pedant of a schoolmaster? Last autumn, as it happened, a scholar who was coming from the capital with a tax official caught dysentery from the heat on the road. He was left behind here, and thanks to the people here, who tended him with all their strength, through winter and into spring he recovered fully. That gentleman's writing is out of this world, and besides he can write Manchu script, and was willing to stay on. He has opened a school here for a year or two and taught this hamlet's children, to repay our great kindness in curing him; he is presently seated in the Guan Yu temple hall." I said, "Could I trouble you to guide me for a moment?" The innkeeper said, "There is no need to ask anyone to guide you." He raised his hand and pointed: "That big temple hall sticking up above the roofs there." I asked, "What is this teacher's name?" The innkeeper said, "Everyone in the village calls him Master Fu." I asked, "How old is Master Fu?" The innkeeper said, "Young master, go and ask him yourself." The innkeeper then went into the kang-room and, taking a few dozen red slips of paper, held them out for me to see, saying, "These are Master Fu's own handwriting." Along the left edge of the red paper was written in fine script: "Mr. So-and-so, my honoured kinsman: on such year, month and day, we respectfully invite your honoured carriage to grace our humble banquet with its presence." The innkeeper said, "When we brothers took a son-in-law last spring, we had him write the invitations." The writing on the slips was just about able to form characters, and the characters on the dozens of slips, large and small alike, were strung like pearls on a thread, as though printed from one block.

paragraphs.orig: 意其秀才爲富鄭公苗裔, 卽喚時大, 同去尋那廟堂裡來。 寂無人聲, 周回觀玩, 右廂裡有小兒讀書聲。 俄有一兒開戶, 探頭一張, 因走出, 不顧而去。 余追問童子, 「儞們的師父坐在那裡麽。」 童子道, 「甚麽。」 余曰, 「富先生。」 童子畧不採聽, 口裏喃喃, 拂袖而去。 余謂時大曰, 「那先生必在這裡。」 遂直向右廂, 一推開戶, 有四五副空椅, 並無人跡。 余闔戶恰裁轉身, 那童子引一老者而來, 想是富也。 適纔閒走比鄰, 那童子忙去報客而回也。 乍觀面目, 全乏文雅氣。 余向前肅揖, 那老者不意抱余腰脅, 盡力舂杵, 又把手顫顫, 滿堆笑臉。 余初則大驚, 次不甚喜, 問,「尊是富公麽。」 那老者大喜道, 「儞老那從識僚賤姓。」 余曰, 「吾久聞先生大名如雷灌耳。」 富曰, 「願聞尊姓大名。」 余書示之。 富自書其名曰, 「富圖三格, 號曰齋, 字曰德齋。」 余問,「甚麽三格。」 富曰, 「是吾姓名也。」 余問,「貴鄕華貫在何地方。」 富曰, 「俺滿洲鑲藍旗人。」
paragraphs.reading: 의기수재위부정공묘예, 즉환시대, 동거심나묘당리내. 적무인성, 주회관완, 우상리유소아독서성. 아유일아개호, 탐두일장, 인주출, 불고이거. 여추문동자, 「이문적사부좌재나리마.」 동자도, 「심마.」 여왈, 「부선생.」 동자략불채청, 구리남남, 불수이거. 여위시대왈, 「나선생필재저리.」 수직향우상, 일추개호, 유사오부공의, 병무인적. 여합호흡재전신, 나동자인일노자이래, 상시부야. 적재한주비린, 나동자망거보객이회야. 사관면목, 전핍문아기. 여향전숙읍, 나노자불의포여요협, 진력용저, 우파수전전, 만퇴소검. 여초칙대경, 차불심희, 문,「존시부공마.」 나노자대희도, 「이로나종식료천성.」 여왈, 「오구문선생대명여뇌관이.」 부왈, 「원문존성대명.」 여서시지. 부자서기명왈, 「부도삼격, 호왈재, 자왈덕재.」 여문,「심마삼격.」 부왈, 「시오성명야.」 여문,「귀향화관재하지방.」 부왈, 「엄만주양람기인.」
paragraphs.en: I guessed that this scholar must be a descendant of Fu, Duke of Zheng, and at once called Si-dae, and together we went to look for that temple hall. It was silent, with not a voice; I looked all round, and in the right-hand wing there was the sound of a child reading. Presently a boy opened the door, thrust his head out for a look, then came out and went off without a glance at me. I pursued him and asked the boy, "Is your master sitting in there?" The boy said, "What?" I said, "Master Fu." The boy paid no attention at all, muttered to himself, flicked his sleeves, and went off. I said to Si-dae, "That teacher must be in here." I went straight to the right-hand wing and pushed the door open: there were four or five empty chairs and no trace of anyone. I closed the door and had just turned around when the boy brought an old man, who I supposed was Fu. He had just been strolling over to a neighbour's, and the boy had hurried to announce a guest and come back. At first sight his features wholly lacked refinement. I stepped forward and bowed solemnly; the old man, unexpectedly, embraced me round the waist and ribs and pounded with all his might as with a pestle, and also shook my hand tremulously, his face piled with smiles. At first I was greatly startled, and then not much pleased. I asked, "Are you Master Fu?" The old man said with great delight, "How did you, venerable sir, come to know my humble surname?" I said, "I have long heard your great name, like thunder poured into my ears." Fu said, "I would like to hear your honoured name." I wrote it down for him. Fu wrote his own name: "Futu Sange, my sobriquet is Yuezhai, my courtesy name is Dezhai." I asked, "What is 'Sange'?" Fu said, "It is my name." I asked, "Where is your honoured native place?" Fu said, "I am a Manchu, of the Bordered Blue Banner."

paragraphs.orig: 富問, 「儞老此去 當面駕麽。」 余曰, 「甚麽話。」 富曰 「萬歲爺要當接見儞們。」 余曰, 「皇上萬一接見時, 吾當保奏儞老得添微祿麽。」 富曰, 「倘得如此時, 朴公大德, 結草難報。」 余曰, 「吾阻水留此已數日, 眞此永日難消。 儞老豈有可觀書冊, 爲借數日否。」 富曰, 「無有, 往在京裏時, 舍親折公, 新開刻舖, 起號鳴盛堂。 其群書目錄, 適在槖中, 如欲遣閒時, 不難奉借。 但願儞老此刻, 暫回携得眞眞的丸子, 淸心元, 高麗扇子, 揀得精好的作面幣, 方見儞老眞誠結識, 借這書目未晩也。」 余察其容辭志意, 鄙悖庸陋, 無足與語, 不耐久坐, 卽辭起。 富臨門揖送, 且言,「貴邦明紬可得賣買麽。」 余不答而歸。

paragraphs.en: Fu asked, "Are you going from here to have an audience?" I said, "What do you mean?" Fu said, "His Majesty is going to receive you." I said, "If His Majesty should receive us, shall I memorialize that you be granted a small stipend?" Fu said, "If it should be so, I would owe Mr. Bak a great debt of virtue that even tying grass could hardly repay." I said, "Held up by the water, I have been stuck here several days, and these long days are truly hard to while away. Have you, venerable sir, any readable books to lend me for a few days?" Fu said, "I have none. When I was in the capital, my kinsman Zhe had just opened a bookshop and printing house, and named it Mingsheng Hall. Its catalogue of books happens to be in my bag, and if you wish to pass the time it is no trouble to lend it. But I hope that when you return this time, you will bring some genuine pills, Qingxin pills, and Korean fans, choosing fine ones as gifts for a first meeting; only then shall I see your true sincerity, and it will not be too late to lend you this catalogue." Observing his looks, his words and his bearing, I saw that he was coarse, perverse, common and vulgar, not worth talking to; I could not bear to sit long, and took my leave at once and rose. Fu bowed me out at the gate, and also said, "Can your country's bright silk be bought and sold?" I did not answer and went back.

paragraphs.orig: 正使問, 「有何可觀 恐中暑。」 余對, 「俄逢一老學究, 非但滿人, 鄙陋無足語。」 正使曰, 「彼旣有求, 何可嗇一丸一箑耶。 第不妨借看書目。」 遂使時大 送淸心元一丸, 魚頭扇一柄。 時大卽回, 持掌大幾葉小冊而來。 皆空紙 ,所錄書目, 盡是淸人小品七十餘種, 此不過數頁所錄。 而要索厚價, 其無恥甚矣。 然旣爲借來, 且新眼目, 遂謄而還之。

paragraphs.en: The chief envoy asked, "Was there anything worth seeing? I was afraid you might suffer sunstroke." I replied, "A moment ago I met an old pedant who is not only a Manchu but so coarse and vulgar that he is not worth talking to." The chief envoy said, "Since he has made a request, how can we be stingy with a pill or a fan? In any case there is no harm in borrowing the catalogue to look at." So he had Si-dae send one Qingxin pill and one fish-head fan. Si-dae returned at once, bringing a small booklet of a few leaves the size of a palm. The leaves were all blank paper, and the catalogue entered in them was entirely small pieces by Qing writers, seventy-odd kinds, and this took only a few pages. Yet he demands a heavy price: how shameless! Still, since I had borrowed it, and wanted besides to refresh my eyes, I copied it out and returned it.

paragraphs.en: I copied it out and gave it to the jinsa Jeong, to serve as a guide for searching the bookshops, and sent it back at once. Si-dae went to convey, and was told to say: "These books are all ones that we have in the East, so my master will not look at this catalogue." Si-dae came back and said that Fu, on hearing what he conveyed, wore a rather disappointed look, and gave him a handkerchief. The handkerchief was over two feet long, of new black crepe gauze.

paragraphs.en: I read the Collected Works of Yang Shen, or played go to pass the time. The deputy envoy and the secretary came to meet at the chief envoy's quarters, and again summoned the party to consult widely on plans for crossing the water. After a long time they all dispersed; there seems to have been no good plan.

paragraphs.en: The innkeeper opened the flue of the kang inside, and with a long-handled shovel raked out the ashes. I thereby took a rough look at how kangs are made. First they build up the foundation of the kang a foot and a hand-span high, to make the ground level; then they set broken bricks like go stones as props for the feet, and lay bricks over them, and that is all. The bricks are naturally of one thickness, so that when broken to make props there is never any wobbling; the bricks are naturally of even build, so that laid side by side they leave no gaps. The flue is only as high as will just admit a hand to put in and take out. The props serve one after another as fire-throats. When the fire meets a throat it must leap over it as though pulled; the flame drives the ash, which crowds in thick, and the many throats swallow in turn and pass it on, with no time to spit back, until it reaches the chimney opening. At the chimney opening is a pit more than a jang deep, which in the dialect of our Eastern country is called "dog-seat" (gaejari). The ash, always driven by the fire, falls and fills the pit, and once every three years the whole length of the flue is opened and the ash raked out. The mouth of the stove is dug down a jang into the ground, with the feeding opening facing upward, and the fuel is lit and stuck in upside down.

paragraphs.en: Beside the stove a hole is dug like a big jar, covered above with a stone lid, level with the ground; inside it is hollow and generates wind, which serves to drive and draw the fire's head into the flue's throat, so that the smoke, once lit, does not leak. As for the chimney, a pit like a large jar is dug, and a brick structure like a pagoda is built, as high as the roof; the smoke falls into the jar as though sucked, as though drawn: this method is still more ingenious. In general, if a chimney has a crack, a single thread of wind can put out the fire of a whole stove; hence the reason our Eastern rooms' ondol so often spit fire and fail to warm evenly lies with the chimney. They either coat a wicker basket with paper or make a tube of wooden boards; but where the mud was first set up there is a crack, or the pasted paper wears away, or the wooden tube has a gap, then the leaking smoke cannot be stopped, and one blast of strong wind reduces the chimney to an empty title.

paragraphs.en: I reflected: "In our East families are poor and fond of reading; hundreds and thousands of brothers, all alike, have crystal beads forever hanging at the tips of their noses even in the sixth month. I wish to master this method and spare them the suffering of the three winter months." Byeon Gye-ham said, "The kang method is, after all, strange; it is not as good as our Eastern room method." I asked, "In what way is it not as good?" Byeon said, "How would it compare with laying down four sheets of oiled matting, its colour like fire-crystal, smooth as water-bone?" I said, "That the kang is not equal to the room is true. But as for its method of making the heated floor, if we merely imitate it and apply it to our rooms, laying oiled matting on it, who would forbid us? The Eastern ondol has six faults and no one has explained them; let me try to discuss them. Listen quietly, and don't clamour. They build a bank of mud and set stones as the ondol; the stones differ in size and thickness and are never uniform, so they must pile small gravel to prop up the four corners and stop the tilting, but the stones scorch and the earth dries and is always collapsing: this is the first fault. Where the surface of a stone has hollows, they patch it with thick earth and smooth it level with mud, so the cooking heat does not warm evenly: the second. The fire-channels are high and wide, and the flames do not join: the third. The walls are thin and sparse and always have cracks, wind comes through and the fire runs back, and smoke leaks and fills the room: the fourth. Below the fire-throat there are no successive throats, so the fire cannot travel far and swirls about at the head of the firewood: the fifth. The work of drying it out requires a hundred bundles of firewood, and for ten days one cannot suddenly enter the room: the sixth. How much better to lay a few dozen bricks together with you, so that in the space of talking and laughing we have already built several rooms of warm ondol and lie down on them to sleep!"

paragraphs.en: At night I drank a few cups with the company; the night-watch drum had already sounded deep, and supported in my drunkenness I went back to lie down, in the kang opposite the chief envoy's, with a cloth curtain hung between. The chief envoy was already fast asleep. I, puffing at my pipe, was half dozing when suddenly by my pillow there came the sound of footsteps. I asked in alarm, "Who are you?" He answered, "Doi-nom-iyo" (擣伊鹵音爾幺). The accent was most unlike anything. I shouted again, "Who are you?" He answered loudly, "Your servant is a doi-nom-iyo." Si-dae and the chief envoy's servants all started up together; there was the sound of a slap on the cheek, and he was pushed out the door by the back. He was a guard-soldier, who every night inspects the lodging of the party, counting from the envoys on down before departing; whenever it is deep night and we sleep soundly, we do not notice. That the guard called himself "doi-nom" was utterly hilarious. In our country's dialect, the northern and western barbarians, the Hu, Lu, Rong and Di, are called "doi," which is a corruption of "island barbarians" (dao yi). "Nom" is a lowly term, and "iyo" is a phrase used in addressing elders and superiors. The guard soldiers, after many years of greeting and seeing off our people, have learned the language from us, and being used only to hearing the word "doi," said it. The whole uproar cost us our sleep. Then ten thousand fleas leaped about, and the chief envoy too lost his sleep; we kept the candle burning until dawn.

paragraphs.en: The sixth day, imo (clear). The stream had subsided slightly, so we set out at last. I entered the chief envoy's sedan chair and crossed together with him. More than thirty lower attendants, stripped bare, bore the chair; at mid-stream, where the current was swift, the chair suddenly tilted to the left and nearly fell. How perilous, how perilous! The chief envoy and I clung to each other, and barely escaped being sunk and drowned. On the far bank we looked back at those crossing the water: some rode on men's necks, some supported each other left and right, and some tied wood into a door-leaf and sat on it, having four men carry it on their shoulders. Those riding horses who swam across all lifted their heads to look at the sky, or shut both eyes tight, or forced a smile and made merry. The servants all took off the saddles and carried them on their shoulders as they crossed; I supposed it was for fear of getting them wet. Those who had crossed shouldered them again and went back; I wondered at it and asked, and was told: "If you go into the water empty-handed, your body is light and easily swept away, so you must press your shoulders down with something heavy."

paragraphs.en: Those who went back and forth several times all shivered, because the water vapour among the mountains was very cold. We took our midday meal at Caohekou, the place called Dapdong ("paddy valley"), so named by our people because it is long swampy. The character 畓 did not exist originally; the clerks of the East wrote the two characters for "water" and "field" together as a composite ideograph, and borrowed the sound of 沓. We crossed Fenshui Pass, then Gaojia Pass and Liujia Pass, and lodged at Lianshan Pass. That day we travelled sixty li.

paragraphs.en: That night, a little drunk, I slept lightly, and suddenly found myself in the city of Shenyang. Palaces, city walls and moats, lanes and markets were prosperous and magnificent. I told myself it was a grand sight, and never expected it to be like this; I must go home and boast of it. So I set off, wafting along; ten thousand mountains and a thousand rivers were all beneath my shoes, and I was swift as a flying kite. In an instant I reached my old house at Yagok, and sat under the south window of the inner room. My elder brother asked, "How is Shenyang?" I respectfully told him what I had seen: "Better than what I had heard," praising it endlessly. Looking out beyond the south window, I saw the shade of a locust tree in the neighbour's house, and above the shade a great star, dazzling and flickering. I respectfully asked my brother, "Do you know this star?" He said, "I don't know its name." I said, "This is the Old Man Star," and rose to bow. My brother said, "I have come home only for a moment, to tell all about Shenyang; now I shall go chasing after the journey again." Going out the door and through the hall, I pushed open a gate of the outer corridor, turned my head and looked north: above the roofs I clearly recognised the peaks of Anhyeon. Suddenly I came to a great realisation: "How foolish, how foolish! How shall I enter the palisade alone?" From here to the Border Gate is over a thousand li; who would stop the march and wait for me? So I shouted aloud, unable to bear my regret; I opened the door to go out, but the door-pivot was very tight. I called loudly for Jang Bok, but no voice came from my throat. I pushed the door with all my strength, and one shove woke me. The chief envoy was just calling "Yeonam!" and I answered in a daze, asking, "Where is this?" The chief envoy said, "A moment ago you were talking in your sleep for quite a while." So I sat up, clicked my teeth and slapped my head to summon back my spirit, and felt suddenly refreshed; sorrow and joy together were hard to manage; I could not sleep again, and tossed and turned in thought, until before I knew it dawn had come. Lianshan Pass is also named Yahu Pass.

paragraphs.en: The seventh day, gyemi (clear). After going two li we crossed a stream on horseback. The water was not wide, yet its current was fierce and rapid, even more so than the day before. As we crossed, we drew up our knees and gathered our feet, and sat rigid on the saddle; Changdae gripped the horse's head tight, and Jang Bok held my rump with all his strength; leaning on each other, we prayed for our lives. In a moment came the grooms' cry to the horses, which sounded exactly like "Alas!" The horse-cry is properly "ho-ho" (好護, "take care"), but in Eastern pronunciation it is close to "Alas" (嗚呼). When the horse reached mid-stream it suddenly turned on its side and leaned left; for when water covers a horse's belly its four hooves float of themselves, so it lies down and swims across. My body, unexpectedly, tilted right, and I nearly fell into the water. The tail of the horse in front lay spread floating on the water; I quickly seized the tail, straightened myself and sat up, and so escaped falling. I myself never expected to be so agile. Changdae too was almost struck by the horse's legs, and was in danger for a moment. Suddenly the horse raised its head and stood upright; one could tell that the water was shallow and its feet had touched bottom.

paragraphs.en: We crossed Moyun Pass and took our midday meal at Qianshuizhan. In the afternoon it was extremely hot. Then we crossed Qingshi Pass; on the pass there is a temple to Guan Yu, extremely efficacious. Post-station porters and horse-drivers jostled to get before the offering table and kowtow, or bought green melons to offer; some interpreters too burned incense and drew lots, to divine the good and ill fortune of their lives. There was a Daoist rapping a bowl and begging for money; he alone did not shave his head but bound it in a mallet-knot, like the lay monks (upasaka monks) of our East; on his head he wore a rattan hat, and on his body a robe of wild silkworm gauze, a Daoist robe looking just like what our Eastern Confucian scholars wear, except that the black square collar is slightly different. Another Daoist sold melons and eggs; the melons were very sweet and full of water, and the eggs lightly salted.

paragraphs.en: That night we lodged at Langzishan. That day we crossed two great passes, and travelled eighty li in all. Moyun Pass, also named Huining Pass, is so high, steep and perilous that, they say, it is no less than our country's Macheon Pass in the northern frontier.

paragraphs.en: The eighth day, gapsin, clear. With the chief envoy in the same sedan chair I crossed the Sanliu River, and breakfasted at Lengjing. After going over ten li we turned out around a spur of the hills, when Taebok suddenly bowed, hurried past the horse's head, and prostrated himself on the ground, saying loudly, "The White Pagoda shows itself to pay its respects!" Taebok is the jinsa Jeong's groom. The spur of the hill still blocked the view and the White Pagoda could not be seen. I urged my horse on; after not many dozen paces, just as we cleared the spur, my eyes were dazzled, and suddenly there was a black ball, a lump, bobbing, rising seven times and falling eight. Only today did I know that human life is attached to nothing at all, that one can only go carrying heaven on one's head and treading earth beneath one's feet. I reined in my horse and looked round on all four sides, and without noticing I raised my hand to my brow and said, "A fine place to weep! One could weep here!" The jinsa Jeong said, "Meeting this great vista between heaven and earth, why do you suddenly think of weeping?" I said, "Yes, yes; no, no. The heroes of all ages were good at weeping, and beauties shed many tears; but it never went beyond a few streaks of soundless tears falling onto the collar. I have never heard of a wail that fills heaven and earth, as if bursting from bronze and stone. Men only know that among the seven emotions it is grief alone that produces weeping, and do not know that all seven emotions can make one weep. When joy reaches its extreme, one may weep; when anger reaches its extreme, one may weep; when delight reaches its extreme, one may weep; when love reaches its extreme, one may weep; when hatred reaches its extreme, one may weep; when desire reaches its extreme, one may weep. To vent pent-up gloom, nothing is quicker than sound; weeping in the world is comparable to thunder.

paragraphs.en: "What issues from the utmost emotion, when it issues, hits the mark of reason; how does it differ from laughter? In the meetings of human feeling, men have never gone through this extreme, and have cleverly arranged the seven emotions, pairing grief with weeping. Hence at times of death and mourning they began to force themselves to bawl out words such as "hu-go" (喉苦, "throat-bitter"), while the true sounds and true voices stirred by the seven genuine emotions are pressed down and held back, pent-up between heaven and earth, and no one dares to let them out. That Master Jia, having found no place for it, and unable to hold it in, suddenly let out one long wail in the Xuanshi hall: how could he fail to startle people?" Jeong said, "Now this place for weeping is as vast as that; I too shall follow you in one great lament. But not knowing what to weep for, if we seek it among the seven emotions, which one is being moved?" I said, "Ask a newborn infant. At birth, what emotion does it feel? First it sees the sun and moon, then its parents, and with relatives filling the room, all are delighted; such joy and delight, to the end of old age, has no equal. By reason there should be no grief or anger; by feeling it should rejoice and laugh; but instead it cries without end, with fury and resentment filling its breast. People will say: 'Human life, whether sage or fool, ends alike in death, and in between come faults and blame and a hundred sorts of trouble; so the baby regrets being born and mourns for itself beforehand.' This is wholly not the true nature of an infant. The baby, dwelling in the womb, lies in dark and dim chaos, coiled and cramped; one morning it bursts out into a vast open space, stretching its hands and feet, its heart and mind clear and wide: how could it not give forth true voice and pour out its feelings in full release? Hence we should take the infant's voice, without any pretence, as our model. Climbing to the summit of Birobong and looking out on the Eastern Sea, one could make a place for weeping; going to the Golden Sands of Jangyeon, one could make a place for weeping. Now, facing the Liao plain, from here to Shanhaiguan twelve hundred li, with on all four sides not a single hill, the rim of heaven and the edge of earth joined as if sewn with glued thread, ancient rain and present clouds only a vast blue-grey: one can make a place for weeping."

paragraphs.en: At high noon it was extremely hot. I urged my horse on, passing Gaolicong and Amizhuang, and turned off the road together with Registrar Jo Dal-dong, Mr. Byeon, Rae-won, the jinsa Jeong, and the retainer Yi Hak-ryeong, and entered old Liaoyang. Its bustle and splendour were ten times those of Fengcheng. There is a separate Record of Liaodong. Going out of the west gate we saw the White Pagoda; its construction was ingenious and imposing enough to suit the Liao plain. There is a separate Record of the White Pagoda. The two records are given below.

paragraphs.en: Back in Liaoyang city, carts and horses rumbled, and onlookers gathered into crowds everywhere. Wine-houses with red railings loomed over the main street; one had hung out a gold-lettered wine flag, on which was written, "Hearing the fame, one must rein in the horse; seeking the fragrance, stop the cart awhile." I could certainly take a drink here! The onlookers pressed all the thicker, shoulders rubbing. I had long heard: "This place is full of rogues; first-time travellers, wholly intent on sightseeing and not alert, are sure to lose something. In a past year, an envoy party took many ruffians along as companions; there were some dozens of people, all first-timers, with clothes and saddlery rather showy. While they were sightseeing in Liaoyang, some lost their saddle-armour, some their stirrups, and none escaped disgrace." Jang Bok suddenly appeared with saddle-armour on his head and a pair of stirrups hung at his waist, standing in attendance before me with no trace of shame. I laughed and scolded him: "Why not cover your two eyes?" Everyone who saw him laughed loudly.

paragraphs.en: Returning, we reached the Taizi River, which was just then swollen with flood, and there was no boat to cross in. Going up and down along the river we wandered about in perplexity, when suddenly a pea-pod fishing skiff drifted out from the reed thickets, and another small skiff lay hidden on the sandbar. I had Jang Bok and Taebok and the rest call for a boat in chorus; a pair of fishermen sat at the two ends with lines dangling, the shade of the willows dense, the slanting sun dyeing everything with gold, dragonflies touching the water and swallows skimming the waves; we called a thousand times and shouted ten thousand, and in the end they never turned their heads. We stood long on the sand, the warm air steaming and boiling us, lips scorched and heads sweating, bowels empty and spirits flagging. All my life I have loved sightseeing, and today I truly paid my debt for it.

paragraphs.orig: 鄭君輩爭相嘲謔曰 “日暮道窮 上下飢困 哭之外無他策矣 先生何爲忍住不哭” 相與大笑 余曰 “彼漁人不肯救人 其人心可知 雖陸魯望先生 正合一拳打倒” 泰卜益爲焦躁曰 “今野日垂地欲墮 他處有山 已將昏黑矣” 盖泰卜雖年少 已七次燕行 凡百慣熟 少焉舟子罷釣 收艇底魚籃 短槳蕩到柳陰邊爭出 五六小艇 見漁艇蕩來 亦爭先來到 要索高價 其待人竭急 然後始肯來濟 其情狀可惡 一船只許載三人 每人貰一鈔 艇皆全木刳成 所謂野航 恰受兩三人者是也 共計一行上下恰是十七馬六疋 皆浮河 艇頭執鞚 順河而下七八里 其危有甚於通遠諸渡時也 宿新遼陽映水寺 是日通行七十里 夜極熱 睡中單衿自脫 微有感氣
paragraphs.reading: 정군배쟁상조학왈 “일모도궁 상하기곤 곡지외무타책의 선생하위인주불곡” 상여대소 여왈 “피어인불긍구인 기인심가지 수육로망선생 정합일권타도” 태복익위초조왈 “금야일수지욕타 타처유산 이장혼흑의” 개태복수연소 이칠차연행 범백관숙 소언주자파조 수정저어람 단장탕도유음변쟁출 오륙소정 견어정탕래 역쟁선래도 요색고가 기대인갈급 연후시긍래제 기정상가오 일선지허재삼인 매인세일초 정개전목고성 소위야항 흡수양삼인자시야 공계일행상하흡시십칠마육필 개부하 정두집공 순하이하칠팔리 기위유심어통원제도시야 숙신요양영수사 시일통행칠십리 야극열 수중단금자탈 미유감기
paragraphs.en: Mr. Jeong and the others vied in mocking and jesting: "The day is ending, the road has run out, high and low we are starving and worn; apart from weeping there is no other plan. Why does the master hold himself back from weeping?" We all laughed together. I said, "Those fishermen refuse to rescue people; their hearts are plain to see. Even Master Lu Luwang would rightly have knocked them down with one punch." Taebok grew still more anxious and said, "The sun on this plain is hanging down to the ground, about to fall; in a place with mountains it would already be nearly dark." For Taebok, though young, had been to Yan seven times and was practised in everything. After a while the boatmen stopped fishing, gathered the fish-baskets from the bottoms of their boats, and with short oars sculled out from beside the willows; five or six small skiffs came out racing one another, and when they saw the fishing boat coming, they too raced up, demanding high fares. They waited until people were in dire extremity before they would consent to come to the rescue, and their manner was detestable. One boat would take only three persons, with a fare of one chao each. The boats were all hollowed from a single log, the so-called "wild boats," that just take two or three people. In all the party, high and low, there were exactly seventeen and six horses (the text gives no unit after the seventeen), the horses all swimming the river, with the reins held at the boat's head; we went down with the current seven or eight li, with more peril than at the crossings at Tongyuan. We lodged at Yingshui Temple in New Liaoyang. That day we travelled seventy li in all. The night was extremely hot; in my sleep I threw off my single quilt, and caught a slight chill.

paragraphs.orig: ## 요동 마을의 풍경
paragraphs.en: Scenes of a Liaodong Village

paragraphs.orig: 初九日乙酉 晴 極熱 乘曉凉 先發歷張家臺三道巴 中火爛泥堡 自入遼東以來 村閭不絶 路廣數百步 沿路兩傍 皆種垂楊 閭閻櫛比處 其對門中間 潦水不洩 往往自成大池 家養鵝鴨千百浮泳 兩邊村舍 盡成臨水樓臺 紅欄翠檻 映帶左右 渺然有江湖之想
paragraphs.reading: 초구일을유 청 극열 승효량 선발역장가대삼도파 중화난니보 자입요동이래 촌려부절 노광수백보 연로양방 개종수양 여염즐비처 기대문중간 요수불설 왕왕자성대지 가양아압천백부영 양변촌사 진성임수루대 홍란취함 영대좌우 묘연유강호지상
paragraphs.en: The ninth day, eulyu, clear, extremely hot. Taking advantage of the dawn coolness, I set out first, passing Zhangjiatai and Sandaoba, and took the midday meal at Lannibao. Since entering Liaodong the villages have never ceased; the road is several hundred paces wide, with weeping willows planted on both sides all along it; where the houses are packed like the teeth of a comb, in the middle opposite the gates floodwater does not drain, and here and there forms great ponds of its own, where households keep geese and ducks by the hundreds and thousands floating and swimming. The village houses on both sides have all become waterside pavilions, red railings and green balustrades reflecting left and right; far off, one has the feeling of rivers and lakes.

paragraphs.en: After the military orderlies' third blast of the horn, they must go several li ahead, and the vanguard officers follow after; the orderlies arrive first. I stop or go as I please; each day with Mr. Byeon I set out at dawn in the cool, and before we have gone ten li we meet the vanguard and surely ride side by side, jesting; every day it is like this. Whenever we draw near a village, the orderlies are made to blow the trumpets, and the four grooms together sing the horse-urging chant; from every house women pour out, crowding the doors to watch, old and young alike, all alike in dress: flowers in their hair, hanging earrings, a little rouge and powder, all with pipes in their mouths, and in their hands the stitching of boot-soles with needle and thread dangling, standing in a close crowd shoulder to shoulder, pointing and laughing prettily. Here for the first time I saw Han women; Han women all bind their feet and wear bow-shoes, and their looks are not equal to Manchu women's; Manchu women are mostly flower-faced and moon-graceful. We passed Wanbao Bridge, Yantai River and Shanyaopu, and lodged at Shilihe. That day we travelled fifty li in all. The aides and interpreters on horseback each pick out a concubine for himself; if the Manchu or Han women they see have been claimed first by another man, he does not dare to claim the same one again; the rule of avoidance is very strict, and they call it "mouth-concubines." Often they quarrel, as if angry, scolding and mocking one another; this too is a way to pass the long road. Tomorrow we shall enter Shenyang.

paragraphs.orig: 遼東舊城 在漢襄平遼陽二縣地 秦曰遼東 後入衛滿朝鮮 漢末爲公孫度所據 隋唐時 屬高勾麗 契丹稱南京 金稱東京 元置行省 皇明置定遼衛 今陞爲遼陽州 移城距二十里 爲新遼陽
paragraphs.reading: 요동구성 재한양평요양이현지 진왈요동 후입위만조선 한말위공손탁소거 수당시 속고구려 거란칭남경 금칭동경 원치행성 황명치정요위 금승위요양주 이성거이십리 위신요양
paragraphs.en: The old city of Liaodong stands on the sites of the Han counties of Xiangping and Liaoyang. Under the Qin it was called Liaodong; later it fell to Wiman Joseon; at the end of the Han it was held by Gongsun Du; in the Sui and Tang times it belonged to Goguryeo; the Khitan called it the Southern Capital, the Jin called it the Eastern Capital, the Yuan established a Branch Secretariat there, and the Ming founded the Dingliao Garrison; it has now been raised to Liaoyang Department, and the city has been moved twenty li away and is called New Liaoyang.

paragraphs.orig: 此廢稱舊遼東 城周二十里 或謂“熊廷弼所築也 城古卑狹 廷弼聞敵騎入境 令夷城 淸人恠之 不敢逼及 諜知改築 引兵至城下 新城峨峨 一夜而成 後廷弼去而遼陷 淸人忿其城堅難拔毁其城 以方興得勝之兵 十日而毁 猶未盡”云
paragraphs.reading: 차폐칭구요동 성주이십리 혹위“웅정필소축야 성고비협 정필문적기입경 영이성 청인괴지 불감핍급 첩지개축 인병지성하 신성아아 일야이성 후정필거이요함 청인분기성견난발훼기성 이방흥득승지병 십일이훼 유미진”운
paragraphs.en: This abandoned city is called Old Liaodong; its walls measure twenty li around. Some say, "It was built by Xiong Tingbi. The old city was low and small; when Tingbi heard that enemy cavalry had entered the border, he ordered the city razed. The Qing people thought this strange and did not dare press close; their spies learned that it was being rebuilt, and they led troops to the foot of the city, where a new city towered, completed in a single night. After Tingbi left, Liao fell; the Qing, angry that the city was so strong it was hard to take, demolished its walls; with soldiers in the flush of rising victory, they took ten days to demolish them, and still did not finish."

paragraphs.orig: 皇明天啓元年三月 淸人旣得瀋 又移兵向遼 經略袁應泰方議三路出師 以復撫順 未行而聞虜陷瀋陽 又將向遼 遂開太子河 注水於壕 環兵登埤 淸人陷瀋五日 至遼陽城下 奴兒哈赤者 所謂淸太祖也 自統左翼兵先至 皇明摠兵李懷信等 率兵五萬出城五里而營 奴兒哈赤 以左翼四旗 擊其左 淸太宗我東所謂汗 其名曰洪台時 我國丙丁錄 雜載紅打時 或稱洪他詩 以其音似而各載 如英阿兒臺曰龍骨大 馬伏塔曰馬夫大 是也 引精銳請戰 奴兒哈赤不許 洪台時堅意行 遂留二紅旗 伏城傍覘視 奴兒哈赤 遣正黃旗 鑲黃旗 助洪台時 衝明營之左 四旗兵繼至 天兵大亂 洪台時乘勝追擊六十里 至鞍山 方其戰時 天兵自遼陽西門出 拔淸人所留城傍二紅旗 伏起邀擊 天兵奔回入城 自相蹂踐 摠兵賀世賢 副將戚金等 皆戰死

paragraphs.en: In the third month of the first year of Tianqi of the Ming (1621), the Qing, having already taken Shen, moved their troops against Liao. The Military Commissioner Yuan Yingtai was just then deliberating on sending forces out by three routes to recover Fushun; before they left he heard that the barbarians had taken Shenyang and were about to advance on Liao. So he opened the Taizi River and let its water into the moat, and arrayed troops on the parapets. Five days after the Qing took Shen they reached the foot of Liaoyang city. Nurhaci, the one called Qing Taizu, himself led the left wing and arrived first; the Ming general-in-chief Li Huaixin and others led fifty thousand troops out five li from the city and camped. Nurhaci attacked their left with the four left-wing banners. Qing Taizong, whom in our East we call the Khan, whose name is Hong Taishi (our Records of the Byeongja and Jeongchuk years write it variously as Hongdashi and Hongtashi, each recorded according to its similar sound, just as Yingaerdai is written Yonggoldae and Mafuta is written Mabudae) led the elite troops and asked to fight; Nurhaci did not allow it; Hong Taishi was determined to go, and so left two red banners in ambush beside the city to watch. Nurhaci sent the Plain Yellow Banner and the Bordered Yellow Banner to help Hong Taishi, and they charged the left of the Ming camp, with the troops of the four banners following, throwing the Heavenly Army into great disorder. Hong Taishi, riding on his victory, pursued for sixty li to Anshan. Just as the battle was being fought, the Heavenly troops sallied from Liaoyang's west gate to take the two red banners that the Qing had left beside the city; the ambush rose and cut them off; the Heavenly troops fled back into the city, trampling one another; the general-in-chief He Shixian, the vice-commander Qi Jin and the rest all died fighting.

paragraphs.orig: 詰朝奴兒哈赤 率貝勒左四旗兵 掘城西閘口 以洩湖水 且令右四旗兵 塞城東進水口 自引右翼 布楯車堵列城邊 囊土運石以壅水 天兵步騎三萬出東門 列營相拒 淸人方欲奪橋 會水口壅遏將涸 四旗前隊渡壕 大呼掩擊東門外天兵 方力戰 淸紅甲二百 白旗千 進擊天兵 死者壕塹皆滿 奪武靖門橋 分擊守壕天兵 城上發火器 聯綿不絶 淸人奮勇衝突 樹梯登城 遂奪西城一面 驅斬民衆 城中擾亂 是夜城內天兵 列炬拒戰 牛維曜等 縋城亂遁

paragraphs.en: At dawn next day Nurhaci led the four left banners with the beile and dug open the sluice at the west of the city to drain the lake water, and ordered the four right banners to block the water inlet at the east of the city; he himself led the right wing, set out shield-carts in rows along the edge of the city, and carried earth in sacks and stones to dam the water. The Heavenly Army, thirty thousand foot and horse, came out of the east gate and drew up camps to confront them. The Qing were about to seize the bridge, when the water, dammed at the inlet, was nearly drying up; the vanguard of the four banners crossed the moat and with great shouts attacked the Heavenly troops outside the east gate, who fought hard; two hundred Qing in red armour and a thousand of the White Banner pressed the attack on the Heavenly troops, and the dead filled the moat entirely; they seized the bridge of Wujing Gate, and split up to attack the troops defending the moat; from the walls firearms discharged without a break; the Qing charged with fury, set up ladders and climbed the walls, and so seized one face of the west wall, driving and slaughtering the people; the city was in uproar. That night the Heavenly troops inside the city raised torches and resisted in battle; Niu Weiyao and others let themselves down the wall by ropes and fled in confusion.

paragraphs.orig: 翌朝 天兵復列楯大戰 淸四旗兵 亦登城 經略袁應泰 登城北鎭遠樓督戰 見城破 擧火焚樓而死 分守道何廷魁 率妻子投井死 監軍道崔儒秀自經 總兵朱萬良 副將梁仲善 參將王豸房承勳游擊李尙義張繩武 都司徐國全王宗盛 守備李廷幹等 皆戰死 生擒御史張銓不屈 奴兒哈赤 命賜死 以遂其志 洪台時惜銓欲生之 婉諭再三 終不可奪 不得已縊而葬之
paragraphs.reading: 익조 천병부열순대전 청사기병 역등성 경략원응태 등성북진원루독전 견성파 거화분루이사 분수도하정괴 솔처자투정사 감군도최유수자경 총병주만량 부장양중선 참장왕치방승훈유격이상의장승무 도사서국전왕종성 수비이정간등 개전사 생금어사장전불굴 노아합적 명사사 이수기지 홍태시석전욕생지 완유재삼 종불가탈 부득이액이장지
paragraphs.en: Next morning the Heavenly troops again drew up shields in a great battle; the Qing four-banner troops also climbed the wall. The Military Commissioner Yuan Yingtai climbed the Zhenyuan Tower in the north of the city to direct the battle, and seeing the city broken, set fire to the tower and died. The defence circuit intendant He Tingkui, with his wife and children, threw himself into a well and died; the military inspector Cui Ruxiu hanged himself; the general-in-chief Zhu Wanliang, the vice-commander Liang Zhongshan, the colonels Wang Zhi and Fang Chengxun, the mobile commanders Li Shangyi and Zhang Shengwu, the military commissioners Xu Guoquan and Wang Zongsheng, the garrison commander Li Tinggan and others all died fighting. The imperial censor Zhang Quan was captured alive and would not submit; Nurhaci ordered that he be granted death, to fulfil his purpose; Hong Taishi, sparing Quan, wished to keep him alive and urged him gently again and again, but in the end could not shake him, and had no choice but to have him hang himself and buried him.

paragraphs.orig: 皇帝於昨年己亥 爲全韻詩 詳載陷城始末 且曰 “明臣之不降者 我祖宗尙加恩 而燕京君臣 漠不相關 功罪不明 欲其不亡得乎”
paragraphs.reading: 황제어작년기해 위전운시 상재함성시말 차왈 “명신지불항자 아조종상가은 이연경군신 막불상관 공죄불명 욕기불망득호”
paragraphs.en: The Emperor, in last year's jihai year, composed a poem on the whole rhyme-list setting out in detail the beginning and end of the fall of the city, and said, "Ming ministers who did not surrender were still shown favour by our ancestors; yet the lord and ministers of Yanjing were indifferent and unconcerned, merit and fault unclear; how could they hope not to perish?"

paragraphs.orig: 按明史 “廷弼之不救廣寧也 三司王紀 鄒元標 周應秋 勘廷弼曰 廷弼才識氣魄 睥睨一世 往歲鎭遼而遼存 去遼而遼亡 獨其驕愎之性 牢不可破 今日一䟽 明日一揭 比之楊鎬 更多一逃 比之袁應泰 反欠一死 若誅王化貞而寬廷弼 則罪同而罰異也
paragraphs.reading: 안명사 “정필지불구광령야 삼사왕기 추원표 주응추 감정필왈 정필재식기백 비예일세 왕세진요이요존 거요이요망 독기교퍅지성 뇌불가파 금일일소 명일일게 비지양호 갱다일도 비지원응태 반흠일사 약주왕화정이관정필 칙죄동이벌이야
paragraphs.en: According to the History of the Ming: "When Tingbi did not relieve Guangning, the three judicial offices, Wang Ji, Zou Yuanbiao and Zhou Yingqiu, assessed Tingbi: 'Tingbi's talent, knowledge and spirit look down on a whole age; in past years when he garrisoned Liao, Liao survived, and when he left Liao, Liao was lost. Only his proud and obstinate nature is firm and unbreakable: one memorial today, one report tomorrow; compared with Yang Hao, he has one more flight; compared with Yuan Yingtai, he lacks one death. If Wang Huazhen were executed and Tingbi spared, the crimes would be the same and the punishments different.'

paragraphs.orig: 今其土壁周遭 而甎痕猶存 誦當日三司之勘 足可以想見其爲人 嗚呼 當皇明末運 用捨顚倒 功罪不明 其視熊廷弼 袁崇煥之死 可謂自毁其長城矣 惡可免後代之譏哉
paragraphs.reading: 금기토벽주조 이전흔유존 송당일삼사지감 족가이상견기위인 오호 당황명말운 용사전도 공죄불명 기시웅정필 원숭환지사 가위자훼기장성의 오가면후대지기재
paragraphs.en: Now its earthen walls still circle round, and the traces of the bricks remain. Reciting the verdict of the three judicial offices of that day, one can fully imagine the man. Alas! In the closing years of the Ming, employment and dismissal were turned upside down, and merit and fault were unclear; looking at the deaths of Xiong Tingbi and Yuan Chonghuan, one may say that they destroyed their own Great Wall. How could they escape the censure of later ages?

paragraphs.orig: 引太子河爲壕 壕中有數三漁艇 城下釣者數十人 皆美衣服 貌似遊閒公子 俱城裏市舖人 余巡壕爲觀 其設閘蓄洩之制 釣者一哄持竿而來 向余開語 余畫地爲字 皆熟視笑而去
paragraphs.reading: 인태자하위호 호중유수삼어정 성하조자수십인 개미의복 모사유한공자 구성리시포인 여순호위관 기설갑축설지제 조자일홍지간이래 향여개어 여화지위자 개숙시소이거
paragraphs.en: The Taizi River is drawn in to make the moat, and in the moat were two or three fishing boats; beneath the walls were dozens of anglers, all in fine clothes, with the looks of idle young gentlemen, all of them shopmen of the town. I walked around the moat to look at the sluice and the way the water is stored and released; the anglers all came in a crowd, rods in hand, and spoke to me; I drew characters on the ground, and they all stared at them closely and went away laughing.

paragraphs.orig: ## 요동백탑기
paragraphs.en: The White Pagoda of Liaodong

paragraphs.orig: 遼東白塔記
paragraphs.reading: 요동백탑기
paragraphs.en: Record of the White Pagoda of Liaodong

paragraphs.orig: 出關廟行不半里 有塔白色 八面十三層 高七十仞云 世傳唐尉遲敬德 率師伐高句麗時 所築也 或云 仙人丁令威 乘鶴而歸 見遼東城郭 人民已改 悲嗚作歌 此其令威所止華表柱 非也 華表柱 在遼陽城外不十里而近 亦不高大 所稱白塔者 我東皁隷順口所名也
paragraphs.reading: 출관묘행불반리 유탑백색 팔면십삼층 고칠십인운 세전당울지경덕 솔사벌고구려시 소축야 혹운 선인정령위 승학이귀 견요동성곽 인민이개 비오작가 차기령위소지화표주 비야 화표주 재요양성외불십리이근 역불고대 소칭백탑자 아동조례순구소명야
paragraphs.en: Leaving the Guan Yu temple, I walked not half a li before coming to a pagoda of white colour, octagonal, thirteen storeys, seventy ren high, they say. Tradition has it that it was built by Yuchi Jingde of the Tang when he led an army to attack Goguryeo. Others say that the immortal Ding Lingwei, who returned riding a crane, seeing that the walls of Liaodong and its people had already changed, sang a song of grief, and that this was the ornamental pillar where Lingwei alighted; this is wrong. The ornamental pillar is within ten li outside Liaoyang city, and it is not tall or large either. The so-called "White Pagoda" is a name that the menials of our East came to by glib repetition.

paragraphs.orig: 遼東左挾滄海 前臨大野 無所障礙 千里茫茫 而白塔乃得野勢三分之一 塔頂置銅鼓三 每層檐稜 懸鐸大如汲桶 風動鐸鳴 聲震遼野
paragraphs.reading: 요동좌협창해 전임대야 무소장애 천리망망 이백탑내득야세삼분지일 탑정치동고삼 매층첨릉 현탁대여급통 풍동탁명 성진요야
paragraphs.en: Liaodong has the blue sea at its left flank, faces a great plain in front, with nothing to obstruct, a thousand li of vastness; yet the White Pagoda takes up a third of the plain's commanding sweep. On the top of the pagoda are placed three bronze drums; at the ridge of the eaves of each storey hang bells as large as well-buckets, which ring when the wind moves them, and the sound shakes the Liao plain.

paragraphs.orig: 塔下逢兩人 俱滿洲人 方往寧古塔買藥 劃地問答 一人問古本尙書 又問有顔夫子書 子夏所著樂經否 皆余所刱聞也 以無爲答 兩人者俱少年 初經此地 爲觀塔來也 行忙未及問其名 盖秀才也
paragraphs.reading: 탑하봉양인 구만주인 방왕영고탑매약 획지문답 일인문고본상서 우문유안부자서 자하소저악경부 개여소창문야 이무위답 양인자구소년 초경차지 위관탑래야 행망미급문기명 개수재야
paragraphs.en: Under the pagoda I met two men, both Manchus, on their way to Ningguta to buy medicine. We conversed by drawing on the ground. One asked about the ancient text of the Book of Documents, and also asked whether there was a book by Master Yan, and whether the Book of Music written by Zixia existed; all of these I was hearing of for the first time. I answered that there were none. The two were both young men, passing this place for the first time, and had come to see the pagoda. In the haste of travel I did not manage to ask their names; they were scholars, I take it.

paragraphs.orig: ## 관제묘기
paragraphs.en: The Temple of Guan Yu

paragraphs.orig: 關帝廟記
paragraphs.reading: 관제묘기
paragraphs.en: Record of the Guan Yu Temple

paragraphs.orig: 出舊遼東城 門外有石橋 橋邊石欄 制極精巧 康煕五十七年所築也 對橋百餘步 有牌樓 刻雲龍水仙畵 皆隱起入牌樓 而東有大樓 其下爲文而扁之曰‘樀錦’ 左有鍾樓曰‘龍吟’ 右有皷樓曰‘虎嘯’
paragraphs.reading: 출구요동성 문외유석교 교변석란 제극정교 강희오십칠년소축야 대교백여보 유패루 각운룡수선화 개은기입패루 이동유대루 기하위문이편지왈‘적금’ 좌유종루왈‘용음’ 우유고루왈‘호소’
paragraphs.en: Leaving old Liaodong city, one finds outside its gate a stone bridge, with stone railings along it of extremely fine workmanship, built in the fifty-seventh year of Kangxi. A hundred-odd paces opposite the bridge there is a memorial archway, carved with pictures of cloud-dragons and water-immortals, all in low relief. Entering the archway and going east there is a great tower, below which, in lettering, hangs a plaque reading "Dijin"; to the left is a bell tower called "Dragon's Chant," and to the right a drum tower called "Tiger's Roar."

paragraphs.orig: 廟堂壯麗 複殿重閣 金碧璀璨 正殿安關公像 東廡張飛 西廡趙雲 又設蜀將軍嚴顔 不屈之狀 庭中列數笏穹碑 皆記修刱始末 新建一碑 記山西商人重修事也
paragraphs.reading: 묘당장려 복전중각 금벽최찬 정전안관공상 동무장비 서무조운 우설촉장군엄안 불굴지상 정중렬수홀궁비 개기수창시말 신건일비 기산서상인중수사야
paragraphs.en: The temple hall is magnificent, with double halls and storeyed pavilions, gold and jade-green gleaming. In the main hall is installed the image of Lord Guan; in the east wing, Zhang Fei; in the west wing, Zhao Yun; and also set up is the figure of the Shu general Yan Yan in his unyielding posture. In the courtyard stand several tall tablet-capped steles in a row, all recording the beginnings and ends of the founding and repairs; one newly erected stele records the rebuilding by Shanxi merchants.

paragraphs.orig: 廟中無賴遊子數千人 鬧熱如塲屋 或習槍捧 或試拳脚 或像盲騎瞎馬爲戱 有坐讀水滸傳者 衆人環坐聽之 擺頭掀鼻 旁若無人 看其讀處 則火燒瓦官寺 而所誦者乃西廂記也 目不知字而口角溜滑 亦如我東巷肆中口誦林將軍傳 讀者乍止 則兩人彈琵琶 一人響疊鉦
paragraphs.reading: 묘중무뢰유자수천인 요열여장옥 혹습창봉 혹시권각 혹상맹기할마위희 유좌독수호전자 중인환좌청지 파두흔비 방약무인 간기독처 칙화소와관사 이소송자내서상기야 목부지자이구각유활 역여아동항사중구송임장군전 독자사지 칙량인탄비파 일인향첩정
paragraphs.en: In the temple there were several thousand idle rogues and wanderers, as noisy and heated as a theatre ground. Some practised with spear and staff, some tried their fists and feet; some mimicked a blind man riding a blind horse for sport; there was one sitting reading the Water Margin aloud while a crowd sat round listening; as he read he wagged his head and wrinkled his nose, oblivious to those beside him. Looking at where he was reading, it was the passage of "burning Waguan Temple," but what he was reciting was in fact the Romance of the Western Chamber. His eyes did not know the characters but his mouth was glib, just as in the lanes and shops of our East people recite from memory the Tale of General Im. When the reader paused for a moment, two men plucked the pipa and one rang the double gongs.

paragraphs.orig: ## 광우사기
paragraphs.en: Guangyou Temple

paragraphs.orig: 廣祐寺記
paragraphs.reading: 광우사기
paragraphs.en: Record of Guangyou Temple

paragraphs.orig: 塔南有古刹曰‘廣祐寺’ 滿洲秀才云 “漢時所刱 而唐太宗伐遼時 駐蹕首山 使鄂公尉遲敬德重修”
paragraphs.reading: 탑남유고찰왈‘광우사’ 만주수재운 “한시소창 이당태종벌요시 주필수산 사악공울지경덕중수”
paragraphs.en: South of the pagoda stands an ancient temple called "Guangyou Temple." A Manchu scholar said, "It was founded in the Han, and when Emperor Taizong of Tang attacked Liao and encamped at Shoushan, he had Duke E, Yuchi Jingde, rebuild it."

paragraphs.orig: 世傳古有一邨夫往廣寧 路遇一童子曰 “負我至廣祐寺 寺右十步古樹下 有藏金十萬 可以相報 邨夫負其童子數百里 不終朝而至 旣至視之 乃一座金佛也 寺僧異之 掘寺右十步 果得十萬金 邨夫以其金重修此寺
paragraphs.reading: 세전고유일촌부왕광령 노우일동자왈 “부아지광우사 사우십보고수하 유장금십만 가이상보 촌부부기동자수백리 부종조이지 기지시지 내일좌금불야 사승이지 굴사우십보 과득십만금 촌부이기금중수차사
paragraphs.en: It is handed down that long ago a villager, on his way to Guangning, met a boy on the road who said, "Carry me to Guangyou Temple; ten paces to the right of the temple, under an old tree, is buried gold, a hundred thousand, with which I can repay you." The villager carried the boy several hundred li and arrived before the morning was out; when he looked at him after they arrived, it was a golden Buddha. The temple monks marvelled at it; they dug ten paces to the right of the temple and indeed found a hundred thousand in gold. The villager used that gold to rebuild this temple.

paragraphs.orig: 及讀寺碑 則乃康煕二十七年 太皇太后發帑所建也 康煕皇帝亦甞臨幸 賜居僧織金袈裟 今廢無僧
paragraphs.reading: 급독사비 칙내강희이십칠년 태황태후발탕소건야 강희황제역상임행 사거승직금가사 금폐무승
paragraphs.en: But when I read the temple's stele, it was built in the twenty-seventh year of Kangxi, by the Grand Empress Dowager at the cost of the treasury. Emperor Kangxi also once visited in person, and bestowed a gold-brocaded kasaya on the resident monks. Now it lies abandoned, without monks.

review.notes: Right work (Dogangnok, PD, d. 1805); the edition lines state that only the preface and 24-28 June are shown, ending with the 28 June entry, with no Hogokjang. Dates marked lunar and the Jeongjo style criticism (munche banjeong) hedged; entries checked against the text. Author/context sections added 2026-10-08 and fact-checked by an independent reviewer (batch 1). Translation (2026-11-03) reviewed by an independent content-review agent: First half: Read all 76 paragraphs against orig; no omissions or summarising found. Fixes (0-based paragraph index in the file): en - Chang-dae to Changdae throughout; Nae-won to Rae-won (cousin 來源, kept distinct from 卞 Byeon Gye-ham, matching B); Deung-nyong to Deuk-ryong (transcription style, like Deuk-gong); Yu Hye-pung/Yeongjae (14, 泠齋 was wrongly Naengjae); 11 (云 speech wrongly rendered 'They told me so'); 9 ('For ten days' garbled); 15 (原包 'not even half filled'); 18 (Sanjiang, Aici, rustling); 27 (Li Rubai); 28 (燎羊裘 ... swallowed the singed coat, was reversed); 33 (Dumi River); 34 (杮 = wood chips, not persimmon); 36 (左鑰 lock, bags were not missing); 39 (守直甫古二名 = two pugu on guard, not 'guards'); 41 (royal physician); 53; 55 (各道 = each spoke of old days of study, not 'provinces'); 63 (Nogajae, Jeonggwan); 67; 68; 75 (五渡河: a taizi every five li, not 'within five li'; 宿松店 = Songdian, Chinese place in pinyin). reading - 羡 is 선 not 이 (35 奇羨, 37 慕羨/妬羨); 着裏 착리 (19); 剌剌 랄랄 (19); 祖霖 조림 (27); 吮 연 (52); 精洒 정쇄 (54); rare chars kept raw in readings: 𩴌魀 (42), 𥦔 (47), 𣎒 (48); 蓒芋濼 left as hanja with reading 한우락 (obscure). Remaining doubts, all source-obscure: 55 金子仁/文淳 (rendered 'Gim Ja-in (Mun-sun)'; could be two people, speaker is a visitor whose district was in turmoil); 𩴌魀 rendered contextually as 'rascals'; 𥦔 rendered 'inside it'; 愛刺河 reading 자 vs 랄; 鄭之子產 sentence is truncated in the source and left as 'Zichan of Zheng.'
